Early Medieval Europe. From around 500 to 1000 CE, often called the "Dark Ages," this was the period of Europe's transformation following the collapse of the Western Roman Empire. Barbarian kingdoms replaced Roman authority, the Christian Church became the primary institution of continuity, and feudalism emerged as the organizing principle of power and land. Though literacy declined and cities shrunk, this era laid the foundations for medieval and modern Europe.

This period was marked by the retreat of Roman governmental structures and the rise of Germanic kingdoms: the Visigoths, Ostrogoths, Vandals, and Franks. The Frankish Empire under Charlemagne from 768 to 814 briefly reunified much of western Europe, establishing the template for medieval kingship. In 800 CE, Charlemagne's coronation as Emperor of the Romans attempted to restore imperial continuity, but his empire fragmented after his death, dividing among his heirs.

The Christian Church filled the vacuum left by Roman collapse, preserving literacy through monasteries and providing moral authority to fragmented kingdoms. Monastic communities became centers of learning and preservation; monks copied manuscripts, maintained agricultural innovation, and maintained continuity of classical knowledge through the cultural darkness. Islam's expansion in the seventh and eighth centuries erased Christian North Africa and the Mediterranean as a unified zone, redirecting trade routes eastward. The Battle of Tours in 732 halted Islamic expansion into western Europe, preserving Christendom's territorial base and shaping the continental divide for centuries.

Feudalism developed as a system of reciprocal obligations between lords and vassals, replacing large-scale imperial administration with local strongmen. Population declined, cities were abandoned for rural settlements, and long-distance trade contracted sharply. Written Latin fragmented into Romance languages; literacy became the province of clergy and monasteries, leaving most of the population illiterate.
